lesson_title: Profitable and Broke: Cash Budgets and Projected Income Statements
hook_text: Best month she ever had. Couldn't pay the wages. Both true.
clip_script: Your cousin does hair. In March she does forty heads — R8 000 of work. Ask her how the month went and she says: strong. But half those clients said “I'll pay you next month”. So on the thirty-first she's holding R4 000 in cash and R4 000 in promises. Did she EARN well? Yes — R8 000, the work is done. Can she buy stock on the first? Only R4 000 says yes. Two honest answers about one month — and that's why a business keeps TWO forecasts. One says what the months will earn. One says what will actually be in the bank. Now scale it up: a shop has its best month ever, R300 000, mostly on credit. The stock was paid for last month. Wages went out. The owner bought a bakkie for cash. And the customers who owe R180 000? They pay in April. The account runs dry in a month the business was WINNING. Profit tells you whether a business deserves to survive. Cash tells you whether it will.
visual_style: A salon chair and a till: coins stacking to R4 000 beside a fan of IOU slips; then a shop's soaring sales bar rising while a bank-balance line dives beneath it, crossing at an empty wage envelope.
mood: Sobering, practical, protective of small businesses.
pacing: Personal open, one clean contrast, escalating to the shop, hard landing on the last line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and forecast both — earnings and cash.
